This means you cannot sync data between devices when self‑hosting. To deploy the offline‑only frontend at your own URL, follow these steps. 1. Clone/Fork this repository 2. This is a turbo repo with `/apps` folder containing apps that can be deployed. Choose the app sub-folder corresponding to the app you want to run. 3. Set the environment variables. 4. Deploy to the provider of your choice ```env VITE_PRODUCT={{memotron | pointron | nucleum }} VITE_STATIC_URL=https://cdn.21n.co ``` _Full app deployment including backend will be available soon..._ ## Contributing Due to the current size of our team, we are not accepting external contributions at this time. We appreciate your interest and understanding. ### License This project is licensed under the AGPL-3.0 license. See the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file for details. ### Contact For any questions, security reporting or feedback, please contact us at [hello@21n.co](mailto:hello@21n.co). ❤️ We extend our deepest gratitude to all the [OSS libraries and tools](https://github.com/21nOrg/nucleus/network/dependencies) that made this project possible. ## Code organization Product bundles in `apps/` compose user-facing features from `client/features/`. `client/ui/` is the domain-free, portable `@21n/ui` package: `elements` owns atomic controls, `compositions` owns reusable compound UI such as charts, breadcrumbs, nested lists, search controls, and time controls, `actions` owns generic DOM behavior, `icons` owns portable icon assets and rendering, `illustrations` owns portable artwork, `branding` owns pure visual brand assets, and `environment` plus `hosts` provide package-wide integration contracts. Portable UI receives product behavior through props or narrow hosts and remains independent of application state, runtime infrastructure, products, features, DataFn, persistence, schema, and domain state. Product-independent Nucleum behavior shared across features or products lives in named subdirectories of `client/shared-state/` and is imported from `@nucleum/shared-state/*`, including command ports and application events; this package must not depend on application, feature, or product implementations. `schema/` owns cross-layer contracts, `client/datafn/` owns storage and sync, and `services/account/` owns the backend. Application composition lives in `client/application/`; account, settings, sharing, library and other workflows live in `client/surfaces/`; navigation, notification presentation and shortcut execution live in `client/shell`; UI-independent infrastructure lives in `client/runtime/`. State is colocated with app context, runtime, preferences, persistence, shell, or feature owners rather than a generic `client/state` directory. See [client boundaries](docs/architecture/client-boundaries.md) for the current ownership model, [type ownership](docs/architecture/type-ownership.md) for contracts, and [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for maintainer orientation. # Contributor and maintainer orientation As noted in README.md, external contributions are not currently accepted. This guide documents the workflow for maintainers and authorized agents. Start with [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md), [WARP.md](WARP.md), [client boundaries](docs/architecture/client-boundaries.md), and [type ownership](docs/architecture/type-ownership.md). Confirm the active product in `client/products` and `client/config`. Reuse `@21n/ui/elements` for atomic controls, `@21n/ui/compositions` for portable domain-neutral compound UI, `@21n/ui/actions` for generic DOM behavior, `@21n/ui/icons` for portable icons, `@21n/ui/illustrations` for artwork, and `@21n/ui/branding` for pure visual brand assets. UI-wide platform state and dependency-inversion contracts belong to `@21n/ui/environment` and `@21n/ui/hosts`, not under an individual element. Keep a composition shared when credible future reuse is intentional even if it currently has one consumer. The entire UI package must remain independent of application state, runtime, products, features, DataFn, persistence, schema, and domain state; inject product behavior through props or narrow host contracts. Keep product-aware branding and other connected adapters with application composition. The concrete application shell lives under `client/shell`; the generic `client/layout`, `client/branding`, `client/illustrations`, `client/icons`, `client/iconsV2`, `client/commands`, `client/events`, and `client/state` owners are retired. Product-independent app-context, appearance, command, event, file, notification, preference, resource, and shortcut behavior belongs to named `@nucleum/shared-state/*` subpaths, which must not depend on application, feature, or product implementations. Connected notification rendering and shortcut execution belong to the shell, while shortcut settings UI belongs under `client/surfaces/settings/shortcuts`. Use repository scripts for setup, compilation, tests, and builds. Run architecture and type-ownership checks for moves, and include a forward migration when generated database mappings change. Do not modify existing tests without the per-file authorization required by AGENTS.md. PRs should describe the user-visible result, ownership changes, checks performed, and limitations. Do not include secrets, local environment files, build output, or unrelated workspace changes. # Repository guide `AGENTS.md` is the governing agent policy. Read it before changes. The current architecture is documented in [client boundaries](docs/architecture/client-boundaries.md) and [type ownership](docs/architecture/type-ownership.md). ## Organization - `schema/`: cross-layer product/resource definitions, wire contracts, and legacy serialization contracts. - `client/datafn/`: client storage, queries, sync, and DataFn resource adapters. - `client/runtime/`: UI-independent auth/account transport, connectivity, logging, native messaging, audio, and inference. - `client/features/`: shared capabilities such as memory, focus, calendar, collections, and spaces. - `client/products/`: product-specific composition, configuration, and integrations. - `client/config/`: client product identity, navigation metadata, and command identifiers. - `client/application/`: composition, lifecycle orchestration, chrome/branding adapters, and startup/action rendering. - `client/surfaces/`: account, subscription, settings, help, sharing, command and library workflows. - `client/shell/`: navigation, panels, tabs, modal chrome, viewport behavior and connected shell presentation. - `client/ui/`: the domain-free `@21n/ui` package. Import atomic controls from `@21n/ui/elements`, reusable compound UI from `@21n/ui/compositions`, generic DOM behavior from `@21n/ui/actions`, portable icons from `@21n/ui/icons`, illustrations from `@21n/ui/illustrations`, pure visual brand assets from `@21n/ui/branding`, portable platform state from `@21n/ui/environment`, and host contracts from `@21n/ui/hosts`. - `client/shared-state/`: the product-independent `@nucleum/shared-state` package with named app-context, appearance, commands, events, files, notifications, preferences, resources, and shortcuts owners. - `client/persistence/`: persistence helpers and legacy backup/recovery boundaries. - `services/account/`: AuthFn/DataFn account service, database mappings, lookup integrations, and Node/Worker deployments. - `shared/`: cross-layer utilities and remaining legacy database objects. - `apps/`, `extensions/`: deployable product and extension bundles; `apps/e2e-playwright` owns browser verification. There is no global `client/types`, `shared/types`, or `client/utils` package. Helpers and tests follow their semantic owners; `@21n/utils` is retired. Import contracts from their domain owner. The unused `@nucleum/cx` workspace is retired. ## Composition rules App context does not implement navigation or command execution. Shared state exposes the command port; `client/surfaces/commands` executes commands whose definitions live with their semantic owners and whose ordered registry is assembled in application composition. The application shell changes URL/history and owns connected notification rendering plus global shortcut execution. Shortcut settings presentation belongs under `client/surfaces/settings/shortcuts`. Application and extension shells install command, overlay, resource, renderer, shortcut, recents, icon-asset, and UI-environment hosts through `client/application/composition/resource-hosts.ts` before mounting consumers. Compositions may use elements, actions, icons, illustrations, branding, environment, and hosts; those lower UI layers must not depend on compositions. Nothing under `client/ui` may directly or transitively depend on application state, runtime, shell, products, features, DataFn, persistence, schema, or domain state. Supply connected behavior through props or narrow host contracts and keep the adapter with its application, shell, or feature owner. Product-aware branding is an application adapter over portable brand assets. Do not move a domain-neutral composition merely because it currently has only one consumer. ## Enforced rules

Run `npm run check:architecture`. CI and the root lint command run the same check. It resolves relative imports, source aliases, dynamic imports, and TypeScript import types in TypeScript and Svelte scripts.

- Features cannot import product implementations, surfaces, or application composition; the top-level shell is the only app-level layer features may consume. Surfaces may compose features; features must never import surfaces.
- Surfaces must not import application composition. Product presentation and action rendering enter surfaces through narrow shared-state hosts installed by application composition.
- The application shell is acyclic: `client/shell` must not import application, surfaces, or products, directly or transitively. Product navigation config enters only through `@nucleum/shared-state/product/product-config-host`; concrete chrome (brand/logo, account avatar, search input, bulk-edit bar, offline status, capture, profile section) enters through optional Svelte snippet props wired by the application chrome adapters (`client/application/chrome/`).
- Portable UI cannot directly or transitively import application state, runtime, the application shell, products, features, DataFn, persistence, schema, or domain state.
- Compositions may use elements, actions, environment, and hosts; those lower UI layers cannot import compositions.
- Shared state cannot directly or transitively import application, feature, or product implementations.
- DataFn and runtime files cannot directly import features, products, application composition or shell, portable UI, or shared client state and services.
- Composition calculations cannot import the session singleton.
- A caller outside a capability must use a source file explicitly listed in `tools/check/feature-entrypoints.json`.

The feature entry-point list records the existing public surface, including individual components and type modules; it is not a barrel module. Additions require an explicit contract change. Package exports expose these same paths. Source aliases bypass package exports, which is why the source-level check remains necessary.

## Current architecture contract

Features cannot import product implementations, surfaces, or application composition. The application shell is the top-level `client/shell` workspace (`@nucleum/shell`), the only app-level layer features may consume. Cross-feature product surfaces live in the top-level `client/surfaces` workspace (`@nucleum/surfaces`); surfaces may compose features, while features never import surfaces. The portable UI foundation is the single `client/ui` workspace, consumed through `@21n/ui/elements`, `@21n/ui/compositions`, `@21n/ui/actions`, `@21n/ui/icons`, `@21n/ui/illustrations`, `@21n/ui/branding`, `@21n/ui/environment`, and `@21n/ui/hosts`. Compositions may use the other UI layers, while elements, actions, icons, illustrations, branding, environment, and hosts never depend on compositions. The entire package remains independent, directly and transitively, from application state, runtime infrastructure, the application shell, products, features, DataFn, persistence, schema, and domain state. Domain-neutral compositions stay in UI when future shared use is intentional, even with one current consumer. Product-connected behavior enters through explicit props or narrow contracts under `client/ui/hosts`, configured from `client/application/composition/resource-hosts.ts` or supplied by the owning shell or feature adapter. Shared state and utilities cannot transitively load application or feature composition at runtime. Explicit type-only edges are excluded from the shared-runtime reachability rule; cross-capability imports remain permitted through declared public entries, so the complete source graph is not claimed to be acyclic.

`client/shared-state` is the single `@nucleum/shared-state` workspace. It groups product-independent Nucleum client behavior by semantic owner without turning `client/` into a list of service folders. Shared command ports and application events are shared state because they are consumed across features, products, extensions, and application composition; concrete command execution remains application-owned. Shared state may consume lower-level runtime, DataFn, persistence, schema, utilities, and portable UI contracts. They may not consume application workflows or shell implementations, user-facing feature implementations, or product composition, directly or transitively. Consumers import named subpaths such as `@nucleum/shared-state/preferences/preferences.store`; there is no root barrel, `shared`, `core`, generic `state`, or nested generic `stores` bucket.

Focus and memory event contracts live under `client/shared-state/events`; clipper
transport events live under `client/runtime/extensions`. App metadata belongs to
`client/shared-state/app-context`. Surfaces consume application-selected action
rendering and product visuals through named shared-state hosts.

Presentation ownership is separate from navigation ownership. Neutral breadcrumbs and scroll containers live in UI. `client/shell/navigation/components/AppBreadcrumbs.svelte` translates application resource and path metadata into structural breadcrumb items and callbacks. Sidebars, tabs, split views, panels, and trails remain in the application shell when they own URL state, resource resolution, product menus, shell events, or other application orchestration. A component moves to UI only when its public contract can be expressed without product or domain vocabulary.

Application and extension shells configure permanent overlay, resource-action, panel, shortcut, recents, record-renderer, action-renderer, portable action, shortcut, file, environment, logging, and haptic contracts in `client/application/composition/resource-hosts.ts`. Configuration runs from base, user, and extension shells before presentation or command execution. Shell and feature adapters provide view-specific props such as keyboard matching, time scales, and address resolution. Shared Markdown display owns portable parsing; memory owns Markdown editing. Portable file presentation, resource enums, event contracts, and action identifiers no longer depend on capability implementations.

The public feature API is enumerated in `tools/check/feature-entrypoints.json`. Each has a static consumer outside its capability. The checker rejects unused public entries and private external imports. This reduces the previous 154 entries by moving shared contracts and infrastructure to their proper owners without introducing barrels or compatibility paths.

Registered workspaces declare their production source imports. `@nucleum/client` owns lower-level config and runtime; `@nucleum/shared-state` owns product-independent shared client behavior, application context, command ports, and events; `@nucleum/shell` owns the application shell; `@nucleum/surfaces` owns cross-feature product surfaces; `@21n/ui` owns all portable presentation and visual assets. Source workspaces bundled by an app declare co-hosted workspace requirements as peer dependencies; existing build dependencies remain dependencies. Peers describe the host's source compilation requirements without adding artificial Turbo build cycles. This is not a claim that each source package builds or installs independently. The checker verifies both resolved workspace and external package imports; test and story dependencies are outside this production-source check.

The narrow Library now mounts resource panes only after a resource is selected. A dedicated focus-capability test covers the portrait Library in Nucleum and Pointron; a seeded Recents probe verifies visibility before and after reload without page errors. Broader regression results are recorded below separately from the architecture checks.

## Application-state ownership follow-up

Product and application context lives in `client/shared-state/app-context/app.store.ts`. Browser/embed environment context lives in `client/runtime/context.store.ts`; persistent UI preference state lives in `client/shared-state/preferences/ui-state`; legacy product-key migration belongs to `client/persistence/migrations`. URL/history and resource navigation live in `client/shell/navigation/navigation.ts`. Product command lookup/execution lives in `client/surfaces/commands/action-runner.ts`; the permanent shared `CommandHost` contract lives in `client/shared-state/commands/command-host.ts` and is installed from `resource-hosts.ts`. Application-wide events live in `client/shared-state/events`. No old methods delegate to the new owners.

Reactive account session state lives with the account runtime in `client/runtime/account/account.store.ts`. Authentication persistence, bootstrap, sign-in, sign-out, navigation, and DataFn teardown are coordinated by `client/surfaces/account/account-session.ts`. Deletion confirmation and cleanup orchestration live in `client/surfaces/account/account-deletion.ts`; subscription operations live in `client/surfaces/subscription/subscription.ts`; file conversion, thumbnail generation, signing, and local/remote storage live in `client/shared-state/files/file-upload.ts`. OAuth initiation and callback presentation belong to surfaces/account; legacy code exchange belongs to runtime/account.

The connected offline-status indicator lives in `client/application/chrome`; shared elements and the shell do not read account session state. Application composition supplies the indicator to shell chrome.

Product menu persistence lives beside navigation. Tab and sidebar mutations live beside the application shell; generic UI-state persistence belongs to the preferences capability. Shortcut persistence, matching, hints, and the host contract live in `client/shared-state/shortcuts`; global shortcut execution lives in `client/shell/shortcuts`, and shortcut settings presentation lives in `client/surfaces/settings/shortcuts`. Headless notification state lives in `client/shared-state/notifications`, while connected notification rendering lives in `client/shell/notifications`. Focus owns its scheduled notification queue, and the existing native transport delivers messages. Memory owns its word-count and PDF-overlay DOM actions. The unused Markdown action and empty `@nucleum/cx` workspace are retired, including active aliases and workspace declarations.

The former `client/stores`, `client/state`, `client/commands`, and `client/events` directories are retired. App context, appearance, commands, events, files, notifications, preferences, resources, and shortcuts have explicit owners under `client/shared-state`. Runtime environment state belongs to runtime, migration state belongs to persistence, the observable-store implementation belongs to DataFn, and overlay state belongs to the application shell. New state follows semantic ownership and must not recreate a catch-all `stores`, `state`, `shared`, or `core` directory; `client/shared-state` is the single approved shared-state workspace and keeps named owners with no root barrel.

Connected record menus and bulk mutations live in `client/features/records`; shared-state/resources retains selection state and the resource action host contract. DataFn resource selection, storage lifecycle, runtime policy and remote transport have named modules; `datafn.store.ts` owns the live client and lifecycle. Persistence separates client storage, device identity, legacy local storage, and the named legacy-backup operations. URL validation and product host parsing have named cross-layer utilities; memory owns its embed sanitizer, and the legacy Surreal query builder lives with server sync.

## Application composition refinement

### Utility workspace retirement (2026-09-22)

`client/utils` and `@21n/utils` are retired, including their workspace and aliases.
Date arithmetic, parsing, period contracts, timezone lookup, user-date calculation
and file-size conversion are domain-free named modules under `shared/utils`.
Duration presentation belongs to UI time controls, chart formatting to chart
compositions, contextual events to UI environment, and color presentation to
theme. Focus owns session-item ordering; shell owns the existing touch-navigation
behavior. Extension transport lives in runtime/extensions, extension navigation
in client/extensions, PDF previews in shared-state/files, migration tracking in
persistence/migrations, and Dexie search preparation beside its worker.
Tests follow those owners; mixed suites are split without changing assertions.
Do not recreate the workspace or replace it with nested generic utility buckets.

Retirement verification: all 411 client/shared/tooling tests pass across 105
files. The 15 approved suites retain all 161 cases and 342 assertion expressions;
68 relocated function bodies match the pre-move snapshot. All four product
compilers report zero errors (378/301/307/0 warnings). Nucleum and Memotron share
production builds, architecture/type-ownership checks, fixed-wait enforcement,
legacy-runtime enforcement and configured lint pass. Negative controls reject
the old package alias, client alias and relative utility imports. Vite starts,
but the local HTTPS host is unavailable; browser, native and cloud workflows
have not been validated by this retirement pass.

### Organization follow-up (2026-09-22)

The former browser/account/network/UI/general utility modules are retired.
Portable positioning, interaction, color and presentation helpers are owned by
UI; domain-free browser environment, events, clipboard and scheduling helpers
are shared utilities. Runtime owns account tokens/cleanup, HTTP transport,
device identity, geolocation and media codecs. DataFn owns resource filters.
The old persistence API facade is replaced by separate account, subscription,
file, address, app-data and Unsplash transports. JSON response validation belongs
to runtime/network. No compatibility modules remain at the former paths.

Global command definitions live with features, surfaces, shell and products.
`application/composition/global-commands.ts` preserves their original ordering;
the command surface no longer owns a registry of every feature implementation.
Support integration is help-owned. Telemetry SDK mechanics are runtime-owned;
application layers own consent/lifecycle wiring. DataFn owns visibility sync,
with overlapping focus/visibility pulls coalesced per runtime.

Clipper webpage, feedback, toolbar, synchronization and record operations have
separate modules. Library query policy is separate from its reactive pane and
request-race guards. Focus separates snapshot hydration, session items,
completion records and notifications from the active-session coordinator.
Capture separates relation persistence, clipboard interpretation, media
metadata, location and completion policy from capture orchestration. DataFn
separates search-provider, encryption-settings and storage-lifecycle mechanics.
Legacy recovery separates database readers, serialization, identity and record
conversion while retaining its public recovery operations and data formats.

The disconnected shell cache subtree and its unused CacheKey enum are retired.
The type checker records this one explicit retirement and still compares the
other 198 runtime enums to the baseline. The empty legacy workspace and unused
Zoho widget, duplicate PDF comment implementation and touch-drag shim are gone.
`server/` and `shared/dbo` are not wholesale deletion candidates: legacy database
utilities and deployment references remain. Retiring those requires a separate
runtime/deployment migration, not an organization-only change.

Manual verification after local compiler/test/build checks: exercise account
sign-in/setup/profile, command lookup and ordering, library search/pagination and
bulk actions, focus timer transitions and restored sessions, file/web/audio
# Type and contract ownership

Tracked in TIDY-478; coordinated with TIDY-477. Module moves preserve runtime enum values and persisted representations.

## Conventions

Definitions stay beside their implementation unless independent consumers need a neutral contract. Feature contracts belong to the feature and external callers use explicit public entries. Portable UI controls own their structural prop and style types: primitives belong to `client/ui/elements`, package-wide host contracts belong to `client/ui/hosts`, portable platform state belongs to `client/ui/environment`, domain-neutral composition contracts belong to `client/ui/compositions`, generic DOM-action contracts belong to `client/ui/actions`, and visual asset contracts belong with `client/ui/icons`, `client/ui/illustrations`, or `client/ui/branding`. Those contracts must not derive from schema records, DataFn resources, runtime types, application actions, or state interfaces; owning adapters translate domain models at the UI boundary. Keyboard contracts are shared by controls and application shortcuts. Application action contracts belong to client configuration; shared command-host and event contracts belong to `client/shared-state/commands` and `client/shared-state/events`; resource-panel and notification models belong to their named capabilities. Browser ambient declarations live in client/ambient.

Schema owns cross-layer account, subscription, and legacy persistence wire contracts. Shared account contracts must not import client modules. Legacy serialized formats remain distinct from current DataFn records: deriving them from a newer schema would change their accepted shape. Generated AuthFn and DataFn/Drizzle files remain owned by services/account generation scripts and are never manually rewritten. Type-only dependencies use import type; enums used at runtime retain value imports.

The global client/types and shared/types packages are retired, without replacement catch-all packages or compatibility exports. Splits use direct imports to the actual owner. Billing presentation fields remain in surfaces/subscription; wire enums and billing data belong to schema/account. Store interfaces are separated from legacy mutation/filter wire contracts. Markdown validation and responsive text truncation leave shared utilities for their frontend owners.

## Current ownership follow-up

Product menu contracts live in `client/shell/navigation/app-menu.type.ts`. The inventory retains original paths as baseline provenance and updates destinations for current ownership. Portable UI, including both former icon systems, illustrations, and pure branding assets, is consolidated in the `@21n/ui` workspace, and the old elements, components, actions, icons, illustrations, branding, layout, state, and stores workspace aliases are retired. Product-independent cross-capability state, command ports, events, and services use named owners under `client/shared-state`; runtime context, persistent UI preferences, migrations, shell state, and product-aware branding adapters are colocated with their semantic owners. Historical manifest and alias snapshots remain as evidence; `currentPackages` records the 30 current manifests. `@nucleum/client`, `@nucleum/shared-state`, and `@21n/ui` are registered private source workspaces and are not independently publishable builds.

The empty legacy and catch-all client utility workspaces have since been retired; `currentPackages` now records 30 manifests. The current checker validates 383 module dispositions and 198 unchanged runtime enums, plus the explicitly audited retirement of the disconnected shell cache's `CacheKey` enum. No other runtime-enum retirement is exempted.

The following migration checklist and audit evidence describe the TIDY-478 baseline. Current application, navigation, account, file, and command ownership is described in `client-boundaries.md`.

## Execution checklist

- [x] Inventory first-party declarations, imports, packages, aliases, and generated modules.
- [x] Define ownership and migration conventions before edits.
- [x] Complete module colocation and mixed-contract splits.
- [x] Retire global aliases/packages and update all callers.
- [x] Enforce contract ownership and audit schema derivation and exceptions.
- [x] Verify products, services, extensions, shared packages, and relevant workflows.
- [x] Deliver coherent commits and record issue completion.

The inventory records every discovered module, its declarations and consumers, original ownership, and disposition. Locally declared types in implementation modules remain colocated; generated schemas remain generated; explicit type modules are reviewed against their consumers.

## Audit evidence and retained contracts

[type-ownership-inventory.json](type-ownership-inventory.json) records all 383 baseline type modules (1,168 declarations), their consumers and explicit dispositions, all 41 package manifests including nested deployment packages, and 462 exported constants. The baseline is commit `32154c37`; destinations reflect this migration. Embedded types remain beside their implementation. Packages without type declarations were audited for exports and dependencies too. Source aliases are build-time paths; `@nucleum/client` is a private source workspace, not an independently publishable package.

- `schema/account` owns profile and subscription wire data. `EmailParts` has one definition. `IPlan` is an application presentation model. The Apple verification response now has one source in the payment provider.
- `schema/legacy` owns the existing Surreal mutation, query, sync, resource-action and store-data encodings. The store-data enum is shared with query generation; Svelte observable interfaces remain in DataFn. Legacy contracts are not derived from modern database rows because their date unions and projected fields differ.
- `schema/datafn.ts` derives resource names from `nucleumDatafnSchema`; `schema/features.ts` derives resource/relation inputs from `defineSchema`. The installed schema API does not provide a compatible generic record inference helper for legacy UI models. Generated account/AuthFn and DataFn files remain unchanged and are produced by `db:generate` and `datafn:generate`; no authoritative schema changed in this task.
- Client `Resource`, `MetaResource` and `Product` compose schema values with the existing Next overlay. This composition is intentional; backend callers import schema directly. Memory node models include editor projections and legacy serialized dates and remain capability-owned rather than copying generated service database types.
- Native transcription model identifiers (`tiny.en`) and worker model identifiers (`Xenova/whisper-tiny.en`) are different protocols. Both live in runtime/inference, in separate native and worker modules with their original enum values. ImportSource and StepType enums in product import adapters likewise describe different supported inputs. Position types in the PDF annotator and media grid represent different coordinate contracts.
- Keyboard and interaction-mode definitions belong to `client/ui/elements`; package-wide portable host contracts belong to `client/ui/hosts`; resource-panel actions belong to `client/capabilities/resources`. Generic error codes are schema-owned, while user-facing error presentation stays in `client/capabilities/notifications` and application composition. Markdown validation belongs to memory, and responsive truncation belongs to the text primitive; shared utilities no longer import client implementations.
- Existing shared utility tests import the relocated validation/truncation functions directly. Their assertions remain unchanged; moving test ownership can be considered separately. Architecture production-layer rules exclude tests, but retired aliases are forbidden in tests too.
- The legacy relay request contract now lives with its server endpoint in `server/common/relay/relay.type.ts` and imports only schema-owned resource and query contracts. Server-to-client imports have no exceptions.
- Existing frontend implementation cycles are not claimed to be removed. Type-only imports erase type dependencies; runtime composition and feature API reduction remain coordinated with TIDY-477. This issue enforces cross-layer contract ownership and deliberate feature entries, not complete acyclicity of the application.

## Import and export rules

Import interfaces and aliases with `import type` or named `type` specifiers. Runtime enum uses must remain value imports. Do not re-export a moved definition from its former location. Public feature entries are listed in `tools/check/feature-entrypoints.json` and must match the feature package exports. DataFn and schema expose their new contracts directly. Do not create a new generic types package.

`npm run check:architecture` checks static imports, exports, dynamic imports, import types, CommonJS requires and Vitest mock imports. It rejects production schema/shared/server/service imports into client code, rejects all server-to-client imports, and rejects the retired package aliases. Historical specs and append-only `.conduct` reports retain references to the old layout as historical evidence; active guidance and configuration use the new owners.

## Verification

`npm run check:apps` passes for Nucleum, Memotron, Pointron and Timear with zero errors (379, 302, 308 and 0 warnings respectively). Account-service typechecking passes. The repository unit suite passes 277 tests with 3 skips; Playwright discovers 549 tests in 55 files. Focus session and Markdown persistence browser probes pass on the local HTTPS Nucleum host.

The share extension production build passes. Its check now reports two pre-existing errors instead of 47: unsupported `aria-label` on the debug-log button component and an optional NodeType at the route boundary. The original commit reproduces both. Timear extension build cannot initialize because the installed Sharp native binary is missing. Account memory integration cannot initialize because installed zod-to-json-schema imports an unavailable zod/v3 export; the original commit reproduces this failure. The separate legacy server suite has identical original/current results: 27 failing suites, 2 passing suites, 9 failed tests, 35 passed and 9 skipped. These include removed legacy Flux imports, missing provider dependencies, real-service integration failures and existing assertions. They are not evidence of migration regressions or passing end-to-end coverage.

`node tools/check/type-ownership.mjs` checks all recorded destinations and compares 199 runtime enum declarations to the baseline. `npm run check:architecture`, `npm run check:no-fixed-test-waits`, `npm run check:no-legacy-runtime`, `npm run lint` and the Turbo build graph dry-run pass. Lint has no package lint scripts and runs the configured static build prerequisite; it is not a claim of repository-wide formatting or ESLint coverage. Existing source aliases remain build-time dependencies; they are not indiscriminately added as workspace dependencies, which would create Turbo cycles. Contract consumers use the schema dependency and the existing frontend package/alias model.

Reproduce the browser checks with `node apps/e2e-playwright/scripts/probe-review-session.mjs` and `node apps/e2e-playwright/scripts/probe-markdown-ownership.mjs` while the local product server is running. Neither requires existing user data; each runs in a fresh offline browser context. Full cross-product Playwright, live auth/sync, native app packaging and production deployment were not exercised.

## Historical overlay/resource ownership refinement

TIDY-477 originally moved reusable popup contracts to the then-current elements package, overlay state to the then-current stores workspace, active-resource/selection state to its resource group, and generic ResourceError to DataFn. The current destinations are `client/ui/elements/modal`, `client/application/shell/overlays`, `client/capabilities/resources`, and DataFn respectively. The default error message belongs to `client/capabilities/notifications`. The inventory destinations follow the current owners so baseline enum validation stays reproducible. See client-boundaries.md for the permanent overlay host contract and the remaining application-specific dependencies.

Those contracts must not derive from schema records, DataFn resources, runtime types, application actions, or state interfaces; owning adapters translate domain models at the UI boundary. Keyboard contracts are shared by controls and application shortcuts. Application action contracts belong to client configuration; shared command-host and event contracts belong to `client/shared-state/commands` and `client/shared-state/events`; resource-panel and notification models belong to their named capabilities. Browser ambient declarations live in client/ambient.

Schema owns cross-layer account, subscription, and legacy persistence wire contracts. Shared account contracts must not import client modules. Legacy serialized formats remain distinct from current DataFn records: deriving them from a newer schema would change their accepted shape. Generated AuthFn and DataFn/Drizzle files remain owned by services/account generation scripts and are never manually rewritten. Type-only dependencies use import type; enums used at runtime retain value imports.

The global client/types and shared/types packages are retired, without replacement catch-all packages or compatibility exports. Splits use direct imports to the actual owner. Billing presentation fields remain in surfaces/subscription; wire enums and billing data belong to schema/account. Store interfaces are separated from legacy mutation/filter wire contracts. Markdown validation and responsive text truncation leave shared utilities for their frontend owners.

## Current ownership follow-up

Product menu contracts live in `client/shell/navigation/app-menu.type.ts`. The inventory retains original paths as baseline provenance and updates destinations for current ownership. Portable UI, including both former icon systems, illustrations, and pure branding assets, is consolidated in the `@21n/ui` workspace, and the old elements, components, actions, icons, illustrations, branding, layout, state, and stores workspace aliases are retired. Product-independent cross-capability state, command ports, events, and services use named owners under `client/shared-state`; runtime context, persistent UI preferences, migrations, shell state, and product-aware branding adapters are colocated with their semantic owners. Historical manifest and alias snapshots remain as evidence; `currentPackages` records the 30 current manifests. `@nucleum/client`, `@nucleum/shared-state`, and `@21n/ui` are registered private source workspaces and are not independently publishable builds.

The empty legacy and catch-all client utility workspaces have since been retired; `currentPackages` now records 30 manifests. The current checker validates 383 module dispositions and 198 unchanged runtime enums, plus the explicitly audited retirement of the disconnected shell cache's `CacheKey` enum. No other runtime-enum retirement is exempted.

The following migration checklist and audit evidence describe the TIDY-478 baseline. Current application, navigation, account, file, and command ownership is described in `client-boundaries.md`.

## Execution checklist

- [x] Inventory first-party declarations, imports, packages, aliases, and generated modules.
- [x] Define ownership and migration conventions before edits.
- [x] Complete module colocation and mixed-contract splits.
- [x] Retire global aliases/packages and update all callers.
- [x] Enforce contract ownership and audit schema derivation and exceptions.
- [x] Verify products, services, extensions, shared packages, and relevant workflows.
- [x] Deliver coherent commits and record issue completion.

The inventory records every discovered module, its declarations and consumers, original ownership, and disposition. Locally declared types in implementation modules remain colocated; generated schemas remain generated; explicit type modules are reviewed against their consumers.

## Audit evidence and retained contracts

[type-ownership-inventory.json](type-ownership-inventory.json) records all 383 baseline type modules (1,168 declarations), their consumers and explicit dispositions, all 41 package manifests including nested deployment packages, and 462 exported constants. The baseline is commit `32154c37`; destinations reflect this migration. Embedded types remain beside their implementation. Packages without type declarations were audited for exports and dependencies too. Source aliases are build-time paths; `@nucleum/client` is a private source workspace, not an independently publishable package.

- `schema/account` owns profile and subscription wire data. `EmailParts` has one definition. `IPlan` is an application presentation model. The Apple verification response now has one source in the payment provider.
- `schema/legacy` owns the existing Surreal mutation, query, sync, resource-action and store-data encodings. The store-data enum is shared with query generation; Svelte observable interfaces remain in DataFn. Legacy contracts are not derived from modern database rows because their date unions and projected fields differ.
- `schema/datafn.ts` derives resource names from `nucleumDatafnSchema`; `schema/features.ts` derives resource/relation inputs from `defineSchema`. The installed schema API does not provide a compatible generic record inference helper for legacy UI models. Generated account/AuthFn and DataFn files remain unchanged and are produced by `db:generate` and `datafn:generate`; no authoritative schema changed in this task.
- Client `Resource`, `MetaResource` and `Product` compose schema values with the existing Next overlay. This composition is intentional; backend callers import schema directly. Memory node models include editor projections and legacy serialized dates and remain capability-owned rather than copying generated service database types.
- Native transcription model identifiers (`tiny.en`) and worker model identifiers (`Xenova/whisper-tiny.en`) are different protocols. Both live in runtime/inference, in separate native and worker modules with their original enum values. ImportSource and StepType enums in product import adapters likewise describe different supported inputs. Position types in the PDF annotator and media grid represent different coordinate contracts.
- Keyboard and interaction-mode definitions belong to `client/ui/elements`; package-wide portable host contracts belong to `client/ui/hosts`; resource-panel actions belong to `client/capabilities/resources`. Generic error codes are schema-owned, while user-facing error presentation stays in `client/capabilities/notifications` and application composition. Markdown validation belongs to memory, and responsive truncation belongs to the text primitive; shared utilities no longer import client implementations.
- Existing shared utility tests import the relocated validation/truncation functions directly. Their assertions remain unchanged; moving test ownership can be considered separately. Architecture production-layer rules exclude tests, but retired aliases are forbidden in tests too.
- The legacy relay request contract now lives with its server endpoint in `server/common/relay/relay.type.ts` and imports only schema-owned resource and query contracts. Server-to-client imports have no exceptions.
- Existing frontend implementation cycles are not claimed to be removed. Type-only imports erase type dependencies; runtime composition and feature API reduction remain coordinated with TIDY-477. This issue enforces cross-layer contract ownership and deliberate feature entries, not complete acyclicity of the application.

## Import and export rules

Import interfaces and aliases with `import type` or named `type` specifiers. Runtime enum uses must remain value imports. Do not re-export a moved definition from its former location. Public feature entries are listed in `tools/check/feature-entrypoints.json` and must match the feature package exports. DataFn and schema expose their new contracts directly. Do not create a new generic types package.

`npm run check:architecture` checks static imports, exports, dynamic imports, import types, CommonJS requires and Vitest mock imports. It rejects production schema/shared/server/service imports into client code, rejects all server-to-client imports, and rejects the retired package aliases. Historical specs and append-only `.conduct` reports retain references to the old layout as historical evidence; active guidance and configuration use the new owners.

## Verification

`npm run check:apps` passes for Nucleum, Memotron, Pointron and Timear with zero errors (379, 302, 308 and 0 warnings respectively). Account-service typechecking passes. The repository unit suite passes 277 tests with 3 skips; Playwright discovers 549 tests in 55 files. Focus session and Markdown persistence browser probes pass on the local HTTPS Nucleum host.

The share extension production build passes. Its check now reports two pre-existing errors instead of 47: unsupported `aria-label` on the debug-log button component and an optional NodeType at the route boundary. The original commit reproduces both. Timear extension build cannot initialize because the installed Sharp native binary is missing. Account memory integration cannot initialize because installed zod-to-json-schema imports an unavailable zod/v3 export; the original commit reproduces this failure. The separate legacy server suite has identical original/current results: 27 failing suites, 2 passing suites, 9 failed tests, 35 passed and 9 skipped. These include removed legacy Flux imports, missing provider dependencies, real-service integration failures and existing assertions. They are not evidence of migration regressions or passing end-to-end coverage.

`node tools/check/type-ownership.mjs` checks all recorded destinations and compares 199 runtime enum declarations to the baseline. `npm run check:architecture`, `npm run check:no-fixed-test-waits`, `npm run check:no-legacy-runtime`, `npm run lint` and the Turbo build graph dry-run pass. Lint has no package lint scripts and runs the configured static build prerequisite; it is not a claim of repository-wide formatting or ESLint coverage. Existing source aliases remain build-time dependencies; they are not indiscriminately added as workspace dependencies, which would create Turbo cycles. Contract consumers use the schema dependency and the existing frontend package/alias model.

Reproduce the browser checks with `node apps/e2e-playwright/scripts/probe-review-session.mjs` and `node apps/e2e-playwright/scripts/probe-markdown-ownership.mjs` while the local product server is running. Neither requires existing user data; each runs in a fresh offline browser context. Full cross-product Playwright, live auth/sync, native app packaging and production deployment were not exercised.

## Historical overlay/resource ownership refinement

TIDY-477 originally moved reusable popup contracts to the then-current elements package, overlay state to the then-current stores workspace, active-resource/selection state to its resource group, and generic ResourceError to DataFn. The current destinations are `client/ui/elements/modal`, `client/application/shell/overlays`, `client/capabilities/resources`, and DataFn respectively. The default error message belongs to `client/capabilities/notifications`. The inventory destinations follow the current owners so baseline enum validation stays reproducible. See client-boundaries.md for the permanent overlay host contract and the remaining application-specific dependencies.

# Editing this README

When you're ready to make this README your own, just edit this file and use the handy template below (or feel free to structure it however you want - this is just a starting point!). Thanks to [makeareadme.com](https://www.makeareadme.com/) for this template.

## Suggestions for a good README

Every project is different, so consider which of these sections apply to yours. The sections used in the template are suggestions for most open source projects. Also keep in mind that while a README can be too long and detailed, too long is better than too short. If you think your README is too long, consider utilizing another form of documentation rather than cutting out information.

## Name

Choose a self-explaining name for your project.

## Description

Let people know what your project can do specifically. Provide context and add a link to any reference visitors might be unfamiliar with. A list of Features or a Background subsection can also be added here. If there are alternatives to your project, this is a good place to list differentiating factors.

## Badges

On some READMEs, you may see small images that convey metadata, such as whether or not all the tests are passing for the project. You can use Shields to add some to your README. Many services also have instructions for adding a badge.

## Visuals

Depending on what you are making, it can be a good idea to include screenshots or even a video (you'll frequently see GIFs rather than actual videos). Tools like ttygif can help, but check out Asciinema for a more sophisticated method.

## Installation

Within a particular ecosystem, there may be a common way of installing things, such as using Yarn, NuGet, or Homebrew. However, consider the possibility that whoever is reading your README is a novice and would like more guidance. Listing specific steps helps remove ambiguity and gets people to using your project as quickly as possible. If it only runs in a specific context like a particular programming language version or operating system or has dependencies that have to be installed manually, also add a Requirements subsection.

## Usage

Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can. It's helpful to have inline the smallest example of usage that you can demonstrate, while providing links to more sophisticated examples if they are too long to reasonably include in the README.

## Support

Tell people where they can go to for help. It can be any combination of an issue tracker, a chat room, an email address, etc.

## Roadmap

If you have ideas for releases in the future, it is a good idea to list them in the README.

## Contributing

State if you are open to contributions and what your requirements are for accepting them.

For people who want to make changes to your project, it's helpful to have some documentation on how to get started. Perhaps there is a script that they should run or some environment variables that they need to set. Make these steps explicit. These instructions could also be useful to your future self.

You can also document commands to lint the code or run tests. These steps help to ensure high code quality and reduce the likelihood that the changes inadvertently break something. Having instructions for running tests is especially helpful if it requires external setup, such as starting a Selenium server for testing in a browser.

## Authors and acknowledgment

Show your appreciation to those who have contributed to the project.

## License

For open source projects, say how it is licensed.

## Project status

If you have run out of energy or time for your project, put a note at the top of the README saying that development has slowed down or stopped completely. Someone may choose to fork your project or volunteer to step in as a maintainer or owner, allowing your project to keep going. You can also make an explicit request for maintainers.

# Tidigit Constitution

## Core Principles

### I. Product Context First

Agents MUST confirm the active product context before touching UI or workflow code. They MUST inspect `client/products/*` configurations and the app context exposed from `client/shared-state/app-context` to respect feature gates and product-specific behaviors. Rationale: enforcing product awareness prevents regressions across Nucleus, Memotron, Pointron, and future bundles.

### II. Reuse Shared System

Agents MUST reuse the domain-free `@21n/ui` package and correctly owned state and utilities when delivering changes. `client/ui/elements` is the permanent atomic-control layer, `client/ui/compositions` is the permanent layer for domain-neutral compound UI intended for reuse across capabilities or products, `client/ui/actions` owns generic DOM behavior, `client/ui/icons` owns portable icon assets and rendering, `client/ui/illustrations` owns portable illustrations, `client/ui/branding` owns pure visual brand assets, and package-wide environment and host contracts live in `client/ui/environment` and `client/ui/hosts`. Nothing under `client/ui` may depend directly or transitively on application state, runtime infrastructure, the application shell, products, features, DataFn, persistence, schema, or domain state. Product-connected behavior MUST enter through props or narrow host contracts configured by an application shell or feature owner. Prefer these layers, helpers such as `generateResourceId` and `generateSimpleRandomId`, and correctly owned logic instead of duplicating behavior. Rationale: reuse stays portable only when reusable presentation is independent of Nucleum composition and state.

### III. Safe State & Data Handling

Agents MUST persist preferences with the correct `Preference` enums, sub-variable scopes, and helper APIs. Frontend persistence MUST use the current DataFn runtime and shared resource stores (`client/datafn/`, `client/features/`, and `schema/`) while respecting legacy local persistence, Dexie, and backup/recovery boundaries under `client/persistence`. Remote synchronization MUST align with the account-service DataFn routes, schemas, generated Drizzle mappings, and lookup helpers under `services/account/src/datafn`, `services/account/src/db`, and `services/account/src/lookup`. Rationale: disciplined state management keeps local stores, DataFn sync state, and account-service records consistent across clients and services.

### IV. Verified Delivery via Repo Workflows

Agents MUST run repository scripts (`npm run dev`, targeted Turbo commands, lint, and tests) that correspond to touched surfaces, and document verification steps alongside changes. Code MUST remain free of inline comments while using JSDoc comments for exported symbols, public APIs, and non-obvious functions. Svelte components MUST follow established structure (script, markup, style). Rationale: shared workflows and TDD discipline keep quality high and reproducible.

### V. Security & Secrets Discipline

Agents MUST prevent exposure of credentials or sensitive data. Environment configuration MUST rely on documented variables such as `VITE_PRODUCT`, `VITE_STATIC_URL`, `VITE_ACCOUNT_BASE_URL`, `VITE_ACCOUNT_BASE_URL_TEMPLATE`, `ACCOUNT_*`, `AUTHFN_*`, `DATAFN_*`, `DEBUG_SINK_URL`, `DEBUG_SINK_WRITE_TOKEN`, and cloud credentials required by deployment or lookup integrations. Storage, auth, sync, and observability integrations MUST use vetted helpers in `services/account`, `schema`, `client/datafn`, and Superfunctions packages instead of ad-hoc secret handling. Rationale: consistent security practices safeguard users and hosting environments.

- When debugging account/auth/DataFn behavior, inspect `services/account/src/app.ts`, `services/account/src/auth.ts`, `services/account/src/debug-sink.ts`, `services/account/src/datafn/`, and `schema/` before changing frontend code.
- Update generated DataFn/Drizzle mappings, schema definitions, and migrations carefully, and coordinate application-side schema expectations with `schema/datafn.ts`.
- Keep shared types with their domain owner in `schema`, `client/features`, `client/runtime`, or `client/datafn`, aligning serialization logic with these definitions before modifying APIs.
- Fix account-service, AuthFn, DataFn, SearchFn, or Superfunctions bugs at their source package rather than masking them in product UI code.

### Testing & Verification

- Run relevant Turbo tasks such as `npm run test`, `npm run lint`, or targeted `turbo run <task> --filter=<project>` after significant changes.
- For UI work, consider Storybook or component-specific verification when available; otherwise smoke test the affected product app.
- Document manual verification steps in pull requests when automated coverage is lacking.

### End-to-End Test Organization

- Organize Playwright suites by shared product capability when the same behavior exists in multiple products. Capability suites such as `tests/focus/` and `tests/memory/` MUST run through product projects and model real product differences through E2E contracts instead of duplicated product-specific specs.
- Keep cross-cutting capability workflows at the capability root and group resource-specific workflows in plural resource directories such as `nodes/`, `objectives/`, and `tasks/`. Resource test directories MUST use plural names.
- Keep a scoped spec at the capability root unless more than two test files clearly belong to the same subdomain. Do not create a nested directory such as `settings/` for one or two specs; use root files such as `settings.spec.ts` instead.
- Centralize repeated capability setup and user workflows in a root helper such as `memory-test-helpers.ts` or `focus-test-helpers.ts`. Keep feature-specific assertions and editor interactions in their owning spec rather than growing a generic helper with unrelated behavior.
- Seed durable precondition state through the E2E DataFn seed fixture (`seed.focus`, `seed.memory`, `seed.collections`) when that state is not the behavior under test. Prefer seed options such as `isPinnedForQuickFocus`, `objectiveId`, and `parentId` over command-bar or panel setup for fixtures. Keep creation, Capture, pin, link, or other setup UI only when that UI path or its side effects is what the test asserts.
- Use Playwright tags only for cross-cutting selection that folder or file paths cannot express. Keep tags such as `@smoke`, `@context-menu`, `@bulk-editor`, `@record-page`, `@creation`, `@browse`, `@settings`, and `@auth`. Do NOT add tags that mirror a directory or file (for example `@focus-feature`, `@session-items`, `@presets`) or capability-scoped smoke/feature aliases such as `@focus-smoke` or `@memory-feature`; select those suites with paths (`tests/focus/`, `tests/focus/active-session/session-items.spec.ts`) and combine with `@smoke` when needed (`tests/focus/ --grep @smoke`).
- Assert immediate user-visible outcomes directly after UI actions: verify the resulting resource, selected bucket, or visible product surface. An action completing, a toast appearing, a store or runtime mutation, or a search result matching is not sufficient proof when stronger visible-state evidence is available.
- Assert DOM readiness and visibility with Playwright web-first locator assertions so UI mode and trace snapshots record the asserted element. For any-of readiness, use `expectAnyLocatorVisible`; for correlated UI conditions, use `expect(...).toPass()` with locator assertions inside. Do not poll `locator.isVisible()` or `locator.isHidden()` booleans.
- Use `expect.poll` only for non-DOM values such as runtime state, persistence, URLs, browser APIs, or serialized collections. Retained polls MUST include a diagnostic `message`; when the polled state has a user-visible consequence, follow it with a direct locator assertion.
- When a workflow writes data that is expected to persist, Playwright tests MUST make both assertions in order: first verify the immediate visible UI feedback, then cross a persistence boundary by closing and reopening the owning page or panel or by reloading the app and navigating back, and verify the durable data again. Do not remove the immediate UI assertion when adding persistence coverage; neither immediate in-memory state nor the post-reopen assertion substitutes for the other.
- Prefer accessible roles, stable test IDs, E2E surface contracts, resource contracts, and shared navigation helpers over CSS structure or product-name branching. Avoid fixed waits where a locator, URL, or persisted-state condition can be awaited.
- Keep specs cohesive and split them when unrelated workflows make ownership or failure diagnosis unclear. Do not copy large specs, repeated route setup, or fallback chains into new resource suites when a shared helper or contract can express the behavior once.

### Workflow Discipline

- Plan work with TODO tracking when tasks involve multiple steps, and close items as progress is made.
- Prefer absolute paths for tooling interactions to avoid ambiguity in the monorepo.
- Use repository-aware tooling, including ripgrep and apply_patch, rather than manual edits that bypass formatting expectations.

### Safety & Secrets

- Never commit environment secrets; rely on documented environment variables such as `VITE_PRODUCT`, `VITE_STATIC_URL`, account-service `ACCOUNT_*` / `AUTHFN_*` / `DATAFN_*` settings, and debug-sink `DEBUG_SINK_*` settings.
- Treat user data and analytics integrations cautiously; consult existing stores or services before changing persistence behavior.

### Additional References

- `WARP.md` for automation policies, CLI workflows, and PR review expectations.
- `deployment/README.md` for infrastructure deployment steps.
- Product-specific docs or configs within `client/products/` for feature toggles and navigation.
- Tests under `tests/`, `apps/e2e-playwright/tests/`, package-local `*.test.ts` files, and fixtures such as `apps/e2e-playwright/tests/fixtures/` to understand existing coverage.
- Always validate assumptions by reading nearby code before rewriting patterns, and ask for clarification when unsure.

## Operational Constraints

- Maintain ASCII-only edits unless files already contain extended characters, never introduce inline comments when modifying code, and prefer JSDoc comments for symbol or function documentation.
- During migrations or refactors, agents MUST NOT introduce intermediary scaffolding, compatibility shims, bridge layers, duplicate config/schema entrypoints, or temporary wrapper APIs unless the user explicitly asks for them. Replace old patterns directly with the target architecture, remove obsolete callers and files in the same change, and stop to ask if a temporary bridge appears unavoidable.

### Non-Negotiable Change Rules

- Any agent fixing issues or bugs, or working on new features, MUST NOT modify existing Playwright or unit tests unless the master explicitly permits each modification.
- Agents MUST NOT modify user-facing UI or functionality unless the master explicitly confirms the change.
- Agents MAY add new Playwright or unit tests when working on new features.

## Workflow Expectations

- Perform code discovery before changes to avoid reimplementing behavior and to understand adjacent systems, especially `client/datafn/`, `client/features/`, `schema/`, `client/persistence`, and `services/account/src/datafn`.
- Align UI updates with accessibility and interaction patterns established in shared components.
- When introducing infrastructure or backend changes, review `deployment/README.md` and coordinate account-service, DataFn, lookup-store, and Cloud deployments with application expectations.
- Record manual verification steps whenever automated coverage is insufficient, ensuring reviewers can reproduce validation.
- Evaluate extension surfaces under `extensions/` whenever share flows or browser integrations are affected to keep host app and extension behavior cohesive.

## Governance

The Tidigit constitution supersedes conflicting process documents for automated agents. Amendments require maintainer approval, an updated Sync Impact Report, and simultaneous updates to dependent templates. Versioning follows semantic rules: MAJOR for principle removals or redefinitions, MINOR for added principles or material scope expansions, PATCH for clarifications. Compliance is reviewed during major feature plans and code reviews; violations must be remediated before merge.

### Sync Impact Report

- Version change: 1.10.1 to 1.11.0.
- Retired client/utils and @21n/utils; colocated helpers and tests with semantic owners.
- Removed workspace/alias/dependency entries and updated architecture enforcement and type inventory.

- Version change: 1.10.0 to 1.10.1.
- Corrected stale command ownership guidance to match the implemented surface runner and application registry assembly.
- Updated application/shell charters and architecture documentation for named transports, account screens, telemetry, sync scheduling and decomposed feature workflows.
- Preserved the existing test and user-facing behavior authorization rules.

- Version change: 1.9.0 to 1.10.0.
- Restricted application source to composition, layers, chrome, branding and paint; retired the remaining workflow and experiment directories.
- Assigned mixed-resource rendering and bulk editing to library, sharing to its surface, OAuth and session resolution to account, diagnostics/errors/support to help, and recovery/update workflows to settings. Modal chrome belongs to shell.
- Extracted runtime host/service-worker/native-message mechanics, shared metadata/timezone/file behavior, and product-configured plan access from application layers. Portable map/capture/quick-access presentation remains in UI with named connected adapters.
- Updated the ownership charters, architecture enforcement, retired-path rules and type-inventory destinations together.

- Version change: 1.8.1 to 1.9.0.
- Made the application shell acyclic: `client/shell` no longer imports `application`, `surfaces`, or `products`; the architecture checker enforces the ban symmetrically with the existing features rule, and the demoted `@nucleum/shell` dependencies on those packages are removed.
- Added the narrow product navigation config host (`client/shared-state/product/product-config-host`, registered from `resource-hosts.ts`) as the only product data the shell reads.
- Injected the five remaining chrome couplings (top nav brand/search/bulk-edit/sync status, left nav profile, app-menu capture) as optional Svelte snippet props wired by the new `client/application/chrome/` adapters; stale paths below are amended accordingly.

- Version change: 1.8.0 to 1.8.1.
- Relocated the base/user application layers (`BaseLayer`, `UserBaseLayer`, `UserLayout`, `AuthGuard`, `ModalLayer`, debug layers), the paint roots (`ComponentResolver`, `AppLoadingView`), and `settingsActionMap` from `client/shell` to `client/application`, since they wire the running product together and were never arrangement-only shell.
- Moved product shortcut defaults (`shortcuts.config.ts`) into `client/application/composition`, already consumed through the `ShortcutHost` contract.
- Relocated `resolveTrialDaysLeft` to `client/runtime/account/plan.utils` and the library resource predicates to `client/shared-state/resources/library.utils`, removing the remaining shell imports of features and subscription surfaces.
- Shell paint resolvers now render named actions through the shared-state action renderer host instead of importing application composition directly.

- Version change: 1.7.0 to 1.8.0.
- Renamed the shared client state workspace from `client/capabilities` to `client/shared-state` (`@nucleum/shared-state`), approving that name as the single shared-state home while retaining the named-owner and no-root-barrel rules.
- Lifted the application shell to the top-level `client/shell` workspace (`@nucleum/shell`); it remains the only app-level layer features may consume.
- Established the top-level `client/surfaces` workspace (`@nucleum/surfaces`) for cross-feature product surfaces (account, subscription, onboarding, help, settings, command, search, library) and enforced that features never import surfaces.
- Narrowed `client/application` toward the composition root, modal orchestration, record presentation, and app-specific integrations.
- Synchronized the architecture references and per-layer charter READMEs; retained existing test and UI authorization rules.

**Version**: 1.11.0 | **Ratified**: 2025-09-27 | **Last Amended**: 2026-09-22
